uk-rave.d: After acid house crossed into Britain, warehouse parties and illegal raves ignited the "Second Summer of Love".

hardcore.d: Rave pushed to 150+ BPM with breakbeats and synth stabs, the common ancestor of jungle and happy hardcore.

happy-hardcore.d: The bright side of hardcore: pianos, female vocals and sheer over-the-top euphoria.

gabber.d: The Netherlands' extreme hardcore: 200+ BPM, distorted kick drums and an anti-social aesthetic.

hardstyle.d: Gabber's kick drum plus trance's melody, a big-room sound from the Netherlands and Italy.

breakbeat.d: Electronic dance music built on broken beats, a fixture of 90s UK clubs and advertising soundtracks.

big-beat.d: Breakbeats plus rock samples and hip-hop attitude, the commercial peak of the late 90s.

jungle.d: Accelerated breakbeats, reggae/dub bass and sampling, an invention of Black British dancefloors.

drum-and-bass.d: Jungle's evolution: 170 BPM breakbeats and enormous bass, mainstream in the UK by the late 90s.

liquid-dnb.d: A more soulful, melodic DnB made for headphones and late nights.

neurofunk.d: Technical, dark, cinematic DnB in which sound design is the star.

trance.d: Melody and breakdowns pulled out of techno and house, with long builds engineered for emotional peaks.

goa-trance.d: Indian Goa beach parties meet acid house: psychedelic, dense, layer upon layer.

psytrance.d: Goa's evolution: hypnotic basslines, stacked effects and an energy curve built to last all night.

progressive-trance.d: Slower, more gradual trance that emphasises long atmospheric builds.

uplifting-trance.d: Trance's most sentimental branch: huge melodies, huge breakdowns, huge singalongs.

edm.d: The 2010s American umbrella that turned electro and progressive house into festival main-stage music, spreading drop culture worldwide.

big-room.d: Minimal drops and horn-like synths designed for ten-thousand-capacity arenas.

future-bass.d: Trap drums plus synth chords and vocal chops, a mid-2010s internet pop sound.

hip-hop.d: 1970s Bronx: DJs cut the break from funk and disco records while MCs worked the crowd; it grew from street parties into one of the world's biggest pop cultures.

old-school-hip-hop.d: Early recordings from 1979 to 1984: disco-style beats, simple rhymes, party themes.

golden-age.d: Late 1980s to early 90s: dense sampling, complex lyrics, conceptual albums.

gangsta-rap.d: West Coast street narratives and a violent aesthetic that pushed hip-hop into controversy and the mainstream.

g-funk.d: P-funk samples, slow grooves and synths; Dr. Dre defined the West Coast sound of the 90s.

boom-bap.d: Hard kick drums and chopped samples, the standard sound of underground New York hip-hop.

jazz-rap.d: Jazz samples and a laid-back flow that turned hip-hop into chamber music.

conscious-hip-hop.d: Hip-hop centred on social issues, racial politics and self-education.

southern-hip-hop.d: Hip-hop from the American South: slower tempos, heavier bass, distinctive accents and dances.

crunk.d: High-energy club rap from Memphis and Atlanta: shouted vocals, 808s and minimal hooks.

trap.d: 808 bass, rapid hi-hats and dark synths; it dominated the globe in the 2010s.

drill.d: A trap offshoot from Chicago and London: bleak melodies, sliding 808s and street narratives.

cloud-rap.d: Late-2000s internet rap: atmospheric samples, slow tempos and blurred vocals.

lo-fi-hip-hop.d: Jazz samples, vinyl crackle and slow drums, background music for studying and unwinding.
